name: Structuring a professional Chevron README
summary:
**Conversation Overview**

The person is a developer working on Chevron, a personal C++20 GUI application infrastructure library they are actively building. They described Chevron as a project inspired by an earlier Python project called Flux Runtime Engine (Fluxr), which served as the motivation and foundation for pursuing a more robust version in C++. The conversation was entirely focused on collaboratively drafting and refining the Chevron GitHub README, working through sections sequentially with the person providing strong directional guidance and Claude iterating on drafts.

The session covered nearly every major README section in sequence. The opening "what is this" paragraph was drafted first, using a casual reflective walk-through that leads the reader to understand why the library exists before naming it. A GitHub `[!WARNING]` admonition was added near the top to signal early development and API instability. The "What Chevron Is and Is Not" section was written as prose with an accompanying Mermaid diagram; the person ultimately drew their own version of the component diagram and found it cleaner than Claude's attempts. A subsystem status table was designed with columns for subsystem name, status (Design / In Progress / Implemented / Stable), and notes, covering all major facilities from the components diagram plus spine entities. Supported platforms, GUI frameworks, and license sections were handled briefly. The "taste of usage" section included a conceptual code snippet the person provided showing the actual Chevron bootstrap structure, including `ENTRY_POINT_METHOD_SIGNATURE` and `ENTRY_POINT_ARG_VARS` macros, `ProcessMemoryConfig`, `ProcessThreadConfig`, `WxEngine::Configuration`, factory registration via `guiEngine->windowing().registerFactory()`, and the four-phase lifecycle of `commitGUIEngine`, `initializeGUIEngine`, `mainloopEntry`, and `shutdown` returning a `ProcessExitReport`.

The Architecture Overview section received significant attention. The "Three-Tier Lifetime Hierarchy" subsection was drafted establishing `AppProcess`, `GUIEngine`, and `WindowEnvelope` as the three nested lifetime tiers with a containment invariant. A second architecture subsection on application structure was then drafted, covering how `AppProcess` owns a polymorphic `GUIEngine` abstraction, which hosts windowing infrastructure (dispatcher, coordinator, subsystem), with live windows represented as `WindowEnvelope` instances and user code running inside those windows directly against the chosen framework. The person confirmed the text for that section was good on the first attempt. Discussion then turned to how to diagram the application structure, with the person wanting something visually distinct from nested boxes and evocative of IDE culture, leading to a recommendation of a project-tree / file-explorer style layout using indented tree syntax with pipe-separated engine variant annotations.

Throughout the session the person demonstrated strong compositional instincts and clear opinions about prose quality, pushing back repeatedly when text felt awkward, over-explained a single point, or used poor sentence composition. Key preferences observed: em dashes should only appear where genuinely necessary and never self-induced; prose should flow sentence-to-sentence with natural hinges rather than feeling like stacked declarative statements; diagrams should complement text rather than be captioned by it; length should be calibrated to necessity rather than completeness; and the library's identity should be communicated with confidence and clarity rather than marketing language. The person explicitly corrected Claude several times for misreading their intent, assuming indecision where none existed, implying conflation of distinct concepts, and over-weighting certain topics relative to their importance. The person's own prose contributions (particularly the bootstrapping section) served as the clearest signal of the compositional style they were targeting.

chat_messages.text: I am working on the README of Chevron right now but I am trying to understand from a high-level what are the best/appropriate things to include here that make this README useful to anyone that encounters the repository? I want to understand how I should structure it and what would make it stand out as professional while not over-selling that idea. I want it professionally structured but casual in its delivery in certain areas so that it sticks to the reader. I am after all a developer just like the next person. A professional README for Chevron should feel like: “This project knows exactly what it is, exactly what it is not, and respects the reader’s time.” We already have a very clear architectural identity. The README should communicate clarity and confidence, not marketing. What do you think?

Jamon wants structural guidance on his README rather than the content itself—he's thinking about organization, tone balance, and how to respect the reader's intelligence. He's clearly someone who values architectural precision and has deeply considered what Chevron is and isn't, so I should frame suggestions around clarity and intentional design choices.

The core challenge is that Chevron occupies an interesting space: it's a pre-1.0 C++20 library with a specific philosophy, aimed at developers who need to quickly determine if it solves their problem. A README for this audience shouldn't oversell or use marketing language—it should be direct about what the project is, what it isn't, and who it's for. The structure should probably lead with that clarity, then move into the practical details of how to use it and understand its design philosophy. I'm thinking through what else belongs in the README — a section on subsystem status would be particularly useful for Chevron since it's still evolving, and then I need to make sure each section is genuinely useful rather than just checking boxes. The goal is to give readers exactly what they need to understand the library and decide if it's right for them, without padding it out with unnecessary detail. cally. A simple table showing what's done, what's in design, what's planned. This is honest and professional and respects the reader. Jamon's project is mid-design — readers should know what's stable and what's evolving.

12. **A "non-goals" section** — Chevron has very explicit non-goals (no widget abstraction, no cross-GUI portability at user-code level). Listing these prevents wasted reader time.

Things to avoid:
- Excessive badges
- Marketing language
- Roadmap section that promises specific timelines
- Too many emojis
- A "features" bullet list — those age poorly and read as sales copy
- Comparing to other libraries (unprofessional, easy to get wrong)
- Long contributing section unless you're actually accepting contributions

The tone Jamon wants is professional structure with casual delivery — clean and standard framing, but prose that has personality. The class descriptions in Chevron already nail this: rigorous yet readable, like "It is the conductor, not a musician." That's the voice to carry through.

Since he's asking for guidance rather than a draft, I should outline a recommended structure with rationale for each section, discuss tone and what to avoid, and note what fits Chevron's current state and identity. I'm not writing the README itself, just helping him think it through. asks
- Over-prescribe — he's clearly capable of making the calls himself
- Be sycophantic

For format, this feels like a design conversation that calls for prose with light structure. Headers and bullets work here, but I should keep them minimal and write like a colleague who understands his docs and what he's building.

I'm aiming for medium length — maybe 500-800 words. Substantial enough to actually help with a real design question, but concise enough to respect his time.

I should start by framing what a README needs to do specifically for Chevron: acknowledge it's pre-1.0, design-heavy, and an infrastructure library. Then walk through a proposed structure with brief reasoning for each section. Close with tone guidance and what makes Chevron's README distinct.

On structure itself, a numbered outline makes sense for his needs, but I'll keep the rationale tight — just one or two sentences explaining why each section matters. I'm also thinking about what's uniquely important for Chevron: the non-goals section is unusually critical here because Chevron's identity is partly defined by what it deliberately isn't. I should also note whether to acknowledge that this is a personal project—a brief status line at the top saying the library is in active design with unstable APIs feels right, honest without being self-deprecating. Now I'm settling on the structure: a framing paragraph at the top, then a numbered outline of what belongs in the README, followed by a section on tone and what to avoid, keeping the formatting minimal and prose-focused rather than heavy-handed.For a project like Chevron — pre-1.0, design-heavy, infrastructure-oriented, with a strong architectural identity — the README's job is mostly *triage*. A reader landing on the repo should know within thirty seconds whether Chevron is what they're looking for, what state it's in, and where to go next if they want more. Everything past that is bonus.

Given what you've already written in your design docs, the voice is mostly solved. The class descriptions already have the tone you're describing — rigorous but breathing, clear about boundaries, willing to say "this is not that." The README should sound like the same person wrote it.

Here's a structure I'd recommend, roughly in order:

1. **One-paragraph "what is this"** — A real sentence, not a tagline. Something like: *Chevron is a C++20 GUI application infrastructure library. It owns the mechanics of a modern GUI application — process lifetime, runtime control, window scaffolding, memory infrastructure — so user code can focus on the application itself, written directly against the GUI framework the user chose.* That's the elevator pitch and it does honest work.

2. **A small status line** — something like *"Active design and partial implementation. APIs are not stable."* Don't bury this. It saves people time and signals respect for theirs.

3. **What Chevron is / what Chevron is not** — You already have this in your Chevron.md and it's one of the most distinctive things about the project. Lifting a compressed version of it into the README right up front is exactly the kind of move that makes a reader trust the project on first contact. Be ruthless about brevity here — it should fit on screen.

4. **A small architecture-at-a-glance** — The three-tier lifetime hierarchy (Process → GUI → Window) is the spine of the entire library. A short ASCII diagram of `AppProcess → GUIEngine → WindowEnvelope` with a one-line gloss on each makes the design legible immediately. This is the single most powerful thing you can put in the README because it tells the reader how to *think* about the library.

5. **A taste of usage** — Even a sketch. A short conceptual code block showing the shape of a Chevron app: construct AppProcess, build a concrete engine, register factories through `engine.windowing()`, commit, init, run. It doesn't have to compile today; it has to communicate the shape. Mark it as illustrative if needed.

6. **Subsystem status** — A small table is genuinely useful here because the library is mid-design. Three columns: subsystem, status (design / partial / implemented), notes. This lets people calibrate expectations honestly. It's also the kind of section that ages well because the columns stay the same as the contents fill in.

7. **Supported platforms and backends** — Short, factual. Linux/macOS/Windows; current backend(s); CMake 3.25+, C++20.

8. **Build / quick start** — The minimum: clone, configure, build, run the dev exe. Three or four commands. Anything longer belongs in dedicated build docs.

9. **Where to go next** — Links to the design docs and class descriptions. This is where the heavy material lives, and the README should point at it rather than try to be it.

10. **License** — A line.

A few things I'd specifically *not* put in:

- A bullet list of "features." Features lists age into lies and read like sales copy. Chevron isn't selling itself; it's describing itself.
- A roadmap with dates. Status is fine; promises are a trap.
- Comparisons to Qt, wxWidgets, etc. by name. The "what it is / is not" framing already does this work without naming names, which is more professional and harder to get wrong.
- A contributing section unless you actually want PRs right now. If you don't, a single line is enough.
- Badges, beyond maybe a build status and license. Badge clutter is the visual equivalent of marketing copy.

On the casual-in-places thing: I'd let the casual register show up in the *prose between sections*, not in the section titles or the structural scaffolding. The structure stays formal — `## What Chevron Is` is a section header, not `## So What's This Thing?` — but the prose underneath can be the same voice that wrote "It is the conductor, not a musician." That sentence would feel completely at home in your README. A reader who hits that line knows the project has a point of view.

The thing that will make Chevron's README stand out is exactly what makes your design docs stand out: it commits to a view. Most infrastructure-library READMEs hedge — they want to be everything to everyone, so they end up being shaped like nothing in particular. Yours can be specific. *This is what this is. This is what it isn't. Here is how to think about it. Here is where to go next.* That's the whole job.

chat_messages.text:
Jamon wants the README to walk readers through the foundational details that make a proper C++ GUI application—those atomic, error-prone pieces that aren't worth the time investment when you're focused on building the actual app—so they naturally arrive at the conclusion that a tool like Chevron needs to exist.

The voice should be casual but professional, reflective like he's recalling the frustration, without being explicit or prescriptive. I'm mapping out the specific pain points: choosing a framework, setting up main() correctly, initializing global state, owning the mainloop, deciding where window creation lives, managing object lifetimes, and getting shutdown sequencing right—all the yak-shaving that happens before you can actually build what you set out to build.

The key is evoking the *feeling* of this rather than listing it. The reader should recognize themselves in the scenario: you want to build something real, you pick a framework, and suddenly you're drowning in foundational infrastructure work that has to be done right or everything downstream breaks in mysterious ways. And you haven't written a single line of your actual application yet. That's the moment where it clicks—this is work every well-formed app needs, and doing it from scratch every time is the wrong approach. Chevron exists to solve exactly that.

For the opening, I'm trying to start with the concrete scenario—picking a framework, writing main(), wrestling with who owns the mainloop—and let that walk the reader through the recognition before landing on what Chevron actually is. The draft opening is good but I need to finish it naturally and then compress the whole arc into something that feels reflective and weary but not complaining. Like someone who's been there talking to someone else who's been there. The list works because each item has enough texture to avoid feeling mechanical. I like how "fault line" captures that atomic brittleness—one mistake cascades through everything. The pivot from "this isn't the application" to "this is the substrate" is where the recognition lands, and then Chevron arrives as the solution. Looking at Jamon's voice in the docs, there's this declarative confidence—statements like "Shutdown is not the inverse of startup"—that I should match in tone. The substrate has to be bulletproof every time, and Chevron is built to handle all those load-bearing decisions — framework selection, process lifetime, window management, memory structure — so you're free to focus on what you actually wanted to build instead of wrestling with boilerplate. I think a brief note about the structural choice is useful — specifically the three-beat structure (scenario → pivot → Chevron's role) — so he can react to the structure as well as the words. But keep that brief. I'll present it cleanly with the draft in a blockquote format to make it visually distinct, then offer to iterate without lecturing.Here's a draft that walks the reader into the conclusion through the recognition rather than the announcement. Three beats: the parade of decisions, the pivot, then Chevron lands as the answer to a problem the reader has already mentally arrived at by the time they get to it.

> Every C++ GUI application has to answer the same set of unglamorous questions before it can be a GUI application. Which framework. How `main()` cooperates with that framework. Who owns the mainloop — because most frameworks want to own it themselves, and that has to be decided rather than ignored. Where windows come from, when they're allowed to exist, what happens when the last one closes. How memory is structured. How shutdown sequences. The decisions are small individually and load-bearing collectively, because everything you actually wanted to build sits on top of them. Get any of them subtly wrong and the rest of the application runs on a fault line.
>
> None of this is the application. It is the substrate the application sits on, and it has to be right every time.
>
> Chevron is a C++20 GUI application infrastructure library. It owns those substrate concerns — process lifetime, runtime control, window scaffolding, memory infrastructure — so the application you actually wanted to build is what you spend your time on. You pick one GUI framework, you use it directly, and Chevron handles the mechanics around it.

A few notes on the choices in case you want to push them:

- The enumeration in the first paragraph is sentence fragments on purpose — they read as a parade of decisions rather than a checklist, which is closer to the *feeling* of starting the project than the bullet-list form would be.
- "Small individually and load-bearing collectively" is the line carrying the atomic-nature idea you mentioned. It's the closest thing to a thesis statement in the paragraph.
- "Fault line" is doing the work that the word *atomic* does in your head — every downstream thing rests on these foundations, and a subtle error in one of them propagates everywhere. If you'd rather use *foundation* or *bedrock* or something else, the sentence flexes around it.
- The middle paragraph (two short sentences) is the pivot. It's where the reader is supposed to stop and recognize that the previous paragraph was leading somewhere. Keeping it small makes the turn land harder.
- The closing paragraph keeps the original "what is Chevron" sentence largely intact, then adds the *you pick one framework, you use it directly* line because that's the second half of the philosophy and it deserves to be in the opening rather than wait for the "what it is / is not" section.

Tell me what to adjust — tone, length, the parade items, which beats to compress or expand.

Let me walk through it.

A *subsystem* in this context is a coherent architectural unit of Chevron. Something with a clear identity, its own design (whether documented yet or not), and either a user-facing surface or structural significance to the library. The working bar is "if this fell over, something the reader would care about would break."

That definition pulls in three categories of thing.

The *facilities* from your components diagram. Those are the highest-value entries because they're what the user reaches for: Memory Infrastructure, Thread Infrastructure, Logging System, Windowing System, Window Component System, Dynamic View System, Telemetry Infrastructure, and System Services.

The *spine entities* that organize the lifecycle: Process Lifecycle (AppProcess) and GUI Runtime (GUIEngine). These didn't make the components diagram on purpose, but they earn a place in the status table because the reader needs to know whether the structural backbone is ready, even if it isn't a facility per se.

The *platform abstraction layer* that underlies everything: the macros, OS detection, and architecture detection in `chevron/common/macro_defs.h` and the corresponding CMake plumbing. Including this is optional. You could argue it's invisible enough that the reader doesn't need to track its status separately, in which case it stays out.

What gets excluded: low-level utilities (`utility/math`, `utility/scope`, `utility/function`, the units library), supporting types that exist in service of a subsystem (WindowFactory, WindowInitContext, WindowEnvelope as individuals are all part of Windowing System), and the build/CMake side of the repository.

Status vocabulary, four buckets: *Design*, *In Progress*, *Implemented*, *Stable*. The fourth is aspirational for now since nothing reaches *Stable* until the API has held still long enough to call it that. Most rows will probably land in *Design* or *In Progress* at this stage.

| Subsystem | Status | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |

> Every Chevron application is structured around a single `AppProcess` at its root. AppProcess owns the GUIEngine, an abstraction whose concrete implementation matches the user's chosen GUI framework. The engine hosts Chevron's windowing infrastructure: a dispatcher that creates windows, a coordinator that owns them once they exist, and a windowing subsystem that surfaces these components together as a coherent user-facing API. Live windows are represented by `WindowEnvelope` instances held by the coordinator, each carrying its own per-window infrastructure. The application's behavior lives inside those windows, where the user writes code against the chosen GUI framework directly.

Five sentences walking the structural picture top-down. The verbs deliberately avoid lifetime language: *structured around*, *owns*, *hosts*, *creates*, *surfaces*, *represented by*, *lives in*. The middle sentence is the longest because it carries the three windowing components and their distinct roles, listed in parallel `X that Y` shape so the length stays readable.

Two specific choices worth flagging. The polymorphism of GUIEngine is handled in a single compact clause ("an abstraction whose concrete implementation matches the user's chosen GUI framework") rather than spending a separate sentence on it. The closing sentence retains the philosophy point about user code touching the framework directly. This section is the right place to ground that idea structurally: once the reader knows the application's behavior lives in the windows, the *user-code-uses-the-framework-directly* claim has somewhere concrete to land.

Jamon wants me to figure out the visual approach for the application structure diagram—he appreciated the text explanation, but now we need to nail the design. The main challenge is avoiding the typical nested boxes pattern we already used for components, and making it feel different from the lifetime diagram's vertical/horizontal nesting. The diagram should visually reinforce the concepts it's explaining and ideally evoke how an IDE organizes code to appeal to developer intuition.

Looking at what the diagram needs to show: AppProcess sits at the root and owns GUIEngine, which then hosts the windowing infrastructure like the dispatcher and coordinator. The coordinator manages WindowEnvelope instances, each with their own per-window infrastructure, and user code lives inside those windows. It's fundamentally a hierarchical composition showing ownership and hosting relationships.

IDEs have some really distinctive visual patterns for this kind of thing—file trees with collapsible hierarchies, code outlines showing class and method structure, class hierarchy views. They use vertical indentation to convey nesting, icons to identify entity types, and often monospaced fonts to feel technical. That tree-like structure could be perfect here.

Building a tree diagram... I'm considering whether a tree structure actually feels different enough from nested boxes, and I think it does—the indentation and connectors create a sense of hierarchy rather than spatial containment. I'm also exploring alternative representations like pseudo-code with braces and namespaces, though those risk being confusing since they're not actual code.

The key insight is that a tree diagram can handle all the requirements: showing composition, the polymorphism of GUIEngine with concrete implementations, component naming, and per-window infrastructure. I'm leaning toward a clean hierarchical structure with optional annotations to clarify relationships, and I'm thinking about how to implement this in mermaid. I'm realizing mermaid will always render nodes as shapes, so a hand-drawn diagram or draw.io would let Jamon create the tree structure more naturally. I should also think about whether labeled arrows showing ownership and hosting relationships add value, or if the tree structure with a simple legend explaining the connectors is sufficient.

For my response, I'll engage with the IDE-tree concept, propose a few concrete approaches, maybe sketch out one or two options to make it tangible, and let him decide which direction resonates. Beyond the IDE tree, there are other visual styles worth considering—blueprint diagrams, subway-map flows, exploded views, construction-order flowcharts, or layered stacks—but the IDE tree feels most aligned with his developer-culture angle and most distinct from the lifetime diagram he already has.

The exploded-view approach is intriguing but might be tricky to pull off cleanly in a README. I'm also wondering about a class diagram styled like a code outline, where instead of traditional UML boxes, the entries look like they came from a class navigator. Or even more directly: what if I present it as a file-path or namespace hierarchy, showing the composition structure through indentation and arrows, emphasizing how the components organize together?

I keep coming back to the tree structure though—it's instantly recognizable to developers as code organization, which makes it the strongest candidate. I could sketch out what that looks like, maybe mention a couple of alternatives like an Architecture Decision Record visualization or JSON-like structure, but the tree approach feels like the most universally readable option. The tree structure makes the polymorphism clear through inline annotations—showing the swappable engine variants like `chevron::wx::Engine | chevron::qt::Engine` in a single line rather than branching them out separately, which is a pattern developers recognize from union types. The ellipsis on `WindowEnvelope...` signals there's more detail to unpack there, keeping the diagram readable while hinting at the per-window infrastructure nested underneath.

I could render this as a monospace block to lean into the code-tree feel, or go with something more visually distinctive like a sidebar structure panel similar to what you'd see in an IDE—indentation showing hierarchy with maybe a vertical accent line. That second approach trades simplicity for visual impact, though it needs careful design to avoid looking like a screenshot rather than a proper diagram.

There's also a third option using faux C++ syntax with nested braces to represent the structure, but that risks confusing readers into thinking it's actual code, which creates more friction than it's worth. I'm leaning toward the first approach—the plain tree with the engine-variant annotation. It's instantly readable, scales well if more components get added, and fits the IDE-culture aesthetic without being visually distracting.

Let me verify the formatting here. The bullets each cover a distinct finishing touch and run 1-2 sentences, so they're justified. The opening validates why the tree approach works—developers already parse hierarchical layouts like this every day from their IDEs. It also creates visual separation from the lifetime diagram and the components diagram, which use different organizational principles.

The sketch demonstrates the tree structure clearly, and the breakdown explains what each visual element represents. I've included practical considerations and walked through alternative approaches like an IDE outline panel or code-as-diagram format to show I've thought this through. The recommendation gives a clear final position.

He specifically asked how to structure the diagram, so my response addresses that structural question directly with the tree proposal and reasoning for why it works. Let me double-check the sketch accuracy before sending.

Verifying the sketch... I'm weighing whether to add a node showing where user application code fits in the diagram. The text makes it clear that behavior lives in the windows, but a developer looking only at the tree might not immediately see that connection. Still, adding it could clutter the visual, and the accompanying text already covers it—so maybe the diagram doesn't need to be completely self-contained. I'm deciding whether to include a "Windowing Infrastructure" grouping node to better reflect how I've organized the concept in the text, since treating those components as a cohesive unit makes more sense structurally than showing them as flat children of GUIEngine. I'm wrestling with whether to add a conceptual wrapper node for "Windowing Infrastructure" — it better reflects the text's grouping, but it might mislead readers into thinking it's an actual class rather than just an organizational label. Since ASCII trees don't have good visual distinction for conceptual groupings versus real entities, I could skip the wrapper and use a comment or annotation instead to keep the diagram cleaner. I'm going in circles trying to annotate the grouping—the bracket notation is hard to render cleanly in ASCII and probably awkward in a vector tool too. I should just keep the tree structure simple and let Jamon handle the visual refinements in his own tool rather than overcomplicating the sketch here.The IDE-tree instinct is good. Developers parse tree-style hierarchical layouts faster than they parse nested boxes because that's the shape we read every day in project explorers, code outlines, and namespace browsers. It also visually distances this diagram from the lifetime one (which leans on temporal nesting) and the components one (which leans on grouped containment), which means the reader's eye gets a genuinely new view of the same entities rather than another variation of "things inside other things."

A project-tree shape would look something like:

```
AppProcess
└── GUIEngine                    (chevron::wx::Engine | chevron::qt::Engine | ...)
    ├── WindowDispatcher
    ├── WindowCoordinator
    │   └── WindowEnvelope...
    │       └── per-window infrastructure
    └── WindowingSubsystem
```

The structural facts come through naturally. AppProcess at the root, the engine swappable per framework (the annotation in parentheses carries the polymorphism), three windowing components hosted inside, the envelopes living under the coordinator, per-window infrastructure attached to each envelope. The reader walks it top-to-bottom the same way they'd walk a code tree.

A few finishing touches worth considering. The annotation showing concrete engine variants (`chevron::wx::Engine | chevron::qt::Engine | ...`) is what does the polymorphism work in a single horizontal sliver, no need for a separate branch. Pipe-separated alternatives is a convention most developers will recognize from union types and grammar notations. The `WindowEnvelope...` with ellipsis signals "one or more instances," avoiding the need to draw two or three boxes. The whole thing can be rendered as a monospace block, or hand-drawn or done in a vector tool with light line weights and indentation. Whichever route, the code-tree aesthetic is what's doing the visual work.

A second option, if you want something more visually striking: a code-outline-style sidebar layout, like what JetBrains or VS Code shows in their structure panel. Entities with optional icons or markers, indentation indicating hierarchy, maybe a vertical accent line on the left. Same structural content, more visually distinctive. The tradeoff is that it requires careful design to not read as a screenshot of an IDE pretending to be a diagram.

A third option to back-burner but mention: a code-as-diagram approach where the structure is presented as faux C++ with nested braces (`struct AppProcess { GUIEngine engine; ... }`). Clever but risks being read as real code when it isn't, which is more friction than payoff.

My recommendation is the first one. The plain tree with the engine-variant annotation hits the IDE-culture target, reads instantly, scales if more components get added later, and stays out of the way visually. The other two are interesting but the first one earns the slot by being the simplest version of what you're describing.
